person.name: Phillis_Wheatley
person.summary: Phillis Wheatley was a West African-born American poet who was enslaved in Boston and educated by the Wheatley family. Her 1773 collection Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral made her the first African American author of a published book of poetry.

conclusion: Phillis Wheatley became the first African-American author of a published book of poetry. Her 1773 collection brought her fame in England and the American colonies.

events.date_note: Born in West Africa, most likely in present-day Gambia or Senegal
events.title: Birth in West Africa
events.description: Phillis Wheatley was born in West Africa around 1753.

events.title: Taken to Boston
events.description: At age seven or eight, Phillis was carried to Boston aboard the slave ship Phillis. Peter Gwinn captained the vessel. Timothy Fitch owned it. John Wheatley bought her for Susanna Wheatley. The Wheatley family named her Phillis Wheatley.

images.caption: The slave ship Phillis associated with Wheatley’s arrival
images.creator: Edwardes, A. D.

events.background:
The Wheatley household was a prosperous Boston home with other domestic enslaved workers. Its members treated Phillis’s learning as an unusual accomplishment and displayed her abilities to relatives and visitors. Mary Wheatley began teaching her to read and write. Nathaniel Wheatley also tutored her. John Wheatley’s reputation as a progressive New Englander shaped the family’s willingness to provide an education that was highly unusual for an enslaved girl.

The household’s division of labor gave her time for books and writing. By age twelve, she was reading Greek and Latin classics in their original languages and difficult passages of the Bible. Alexander Pope, John Milton, Homer, Horace, and Virgil became major sources for her poetry. Her first known poem, To the University of Cambridge [Harvard], in New England, came when she was fourteen. The family’s support gave her access to the literary training that later made publication possible.

Her education did not free her from the racial assumptions of colonial Boston. When a proposed volume of her poems sought subscribers in 1772, colonial publishers would not accept it. A London bookseller required evidence that the poems were her own. Eighteen Boston men, including Thomas Hutchinson, Andrew Oliver, John Hancock, John Erving, and Reverend Charles Chauncey, examined her and signed an attestation. The statement described her as having been brought from Africa and serving as a slave in a Boston family. It appeared in the preface to Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral. London patrons then supported the book’s publication.

event_class.title: Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral
event_class.impact: The volume brought Wheatley fame in England and the American colonies. It made her the first African-American author to publish a book of poetry.

events.background:
In early 1772, Boston readers were asked to subscribe in advance to a proposed collection of 28 poems. Subscription commitments commonly financed colonial books by guaranteeing sales before printing. The appeal failed in a culture where many white educated colonists claimed that Black Africans lacked the capacity for literary work. David Hume and Immanuel Kant were among Enlightenment writers who voiced theories of racial hierarchy. Wheatley’s earlier elegy for the evangelical preacher George Whitefield had already drawn attention on both sides of the Atlantic. Selina Hastings had belonged to Whitefield’s parish and maintained a wide Methodist network. She also financed chapels and the training college at Trevecca in Wales.

The finished collection contained 39 poems. More than a third were elegies. Its remaining poems treated Christian devotion, classical subjects, abstract ideas, and prominent people. The prefatory material presented the poems as products of the author’s “leisure Moments” and asked critics not to dismiss their defects. John Wheatley’s accompanying letter told the London trade that she had learned English within his household and had begun Latin. These pages addressed readers who expected an explanation for how an enslaved Black writer could have acquired literary learning.

The book entered a Boston already shaken by Parliament’s Tea Act. Copies sent across the Atlantic were loaded aboard the Dartmouth, one of the vessels later targeted in the Boston Tea Party. Protesters seized the ship’s tea cargo in December 1773. They left the books untouched. A copy is displayed at the Boston Tea Party Museum. The collection went through 11 editions by 1816, while several poems intended for a later volume appeared separately in pamphlets and newspapers.

events.date_note: The Wheatleys manumitted her by November 1773
events.title: Gains Her Freedom
events.description: By November 1773, John and Susanna Wheatley manumitted Phillis Wheatley in Boston.

events.title: Travels to London
events.description: Wheatley traveled to London with Nathaniel Wheatley in 1773. Chronic asthma affected her health. Susanna Wheatley also believed London offered a better chance of publishing her poems. Wheatley had an audience with Lord Mayor Frederick Bull.

events.title: Sends a Poem to Washington
events.description: In 1775, Phillis Wheatley sent General George Washington a copy of To His Excellency, George Washington.

images.caption: Portrait print of General George Washington
images.creator: Charles Willson Peale / Benjamin Blyth

events.background:
By 1775, the American Revolution had turned public language about liberty into a charged subject for an enslaved writer in Boston. Wheatley had already addressed imperial politics in her 1768 poem To the King's Most Excellent Majesty, which praised George III for repealing the Stamp Act. Its language of freedom also raised the freedom of people enslaved under the king. As resistance to Britain intensified, her writing took up ideas associated with the rebellious colonists. Her religious and classical reading gave her a vocabulary shared by educated Atlantic-world readers. She read Greek and Latin classics in their original languages, as well as the Bible, Alexander Pope, John Milton, Homer, Horace, and Virgil.

The recent London volume placed Wheatley's verse before readers on both sides of the Atlantic. Boston publishers had declined to issue the collection. London patrons, including Selina Hastings, Countess of Huntingdon, and the Earl of Dartmouth, helped secure its publication. The book carried an attestation signed by leading Boston men who said they believed Wheatley had written the poems. The document arose from repeated doubts that an African woman held in slavery could be their author. It appeared in the book's preface alongside a deferential statement that the poems had been written in her leisure moments.

## A poem in wartime

The poem addressed to Washington joined formal praise with the immediate language of the revolutionary cause. A year later, Washington invited Wheatley to his military headquarters in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Thomas Paine republished the poem in The Pennsylvania Gazette in April 1776. The newspaper printing put her work into circulation during the war and connected it to a figure commanding the colonial military effort. Washington later wrote that the style and manner of her poetry offered “a striking proof” of her poetic talents.

Wheatley continued to seek an audience after the war began. In 1779, she issued a proposal for a second book of poems. She had lost the patrons who had supported her earlier volume after her emancipation. The Revolutionary War also hindered the subscription sales needed to finance publication. Several poems planned for that volume later appeared in pamphlets and newspapers.

events.title: Marries John Peters in Boston
events.description: Wheatley married John Peters in 1778. Peters was an impoverished free Black grocer. They married shortly after John Wheatley’s death.

events.date_note: Wheatley placed advertisements for subscribers between October 30 and December 18, 1779
events.title: Seeks Subscribers for Second Volume
events.description: From October 30 through December 18, 1779, Wheatley advertised in Boston for subscribers to a second volume of poems. She planned a volume of about 300 pages. She intended to dedicate it to Benjamin Franklin.

events.title: Dies in Boston at Thirty-One
events.description: In 1784, Wheatley worked as a scullery maid at a Boston boarding house. She developed pneumonia after giving birth to a daughter. Wheatley died on December 5. Her daughter died the same day.
events.background:
Boston’s literary market depended on subscriptions, in which prospective buyers promised to purchase a book before a printer took on its cost. Wheatley tried that route in 1772, when she and Susanna Wheatley placed notices seeking subscribers for a collection of 28 poems. No colonial publisher accepted it. White members of the colonial elite commonly claimed that Black Africans lacked the capacity for literary writing. A London publisher required public proof that the poems were hers. Eighteen prominent Boston men signed the attestation included in the printed volume. Selina Hastings, Countess of Huntingdon, subsidized its publication. The book ultimately went through 11 editions by 1816.

Her plans for another book met a far harsher market. The Wheatleys, who had supplied access to patrons and influential readers, were gone by 1778. The Revolutionary War also disrupted the subscription trade on which book publishing depended. Wheatley advertised for a second collection in Boston newspapers in late 1779. She proposed a book of about 300 pages and planned to dedicate it to Benjamin Franklin. No volume appeared.

The surviving poems from that proposed collection later reached readers only in pamphlets and newspapers. Her correspondence had provided another outlet. In a letter to the Mohegan minister Samson Occom, Wheatley supported the natural-born rights of enslaved people in America. She also exchanged letters with the British philanthropist John Thornton, who discussed her poetry with John Newton. By the time the second book failed to find subscribers, the network of patrons, printers, and readers that had carried her work across the Atlantic had largely dissolved.
